guide.title: Van Cortlandt Park, the Bronx: 1,146 Acres, Public Golf and a 1748 House
guide.intro: Van Cortlandt Park covers 1,146 acres (464 ha) in the Bronx, the third-largest park in New York City behind the Staten Island Greenbelt at 1,778 acres and Pelham Bay Park at 2,772 acres. Van Cortlandt Lake, the largest freshwater lake in the Bronx, covers 18 acres and runs 4 to 8 feet deep, fed by Tibbetts Brook, a stream originating in Yonkers which runs through a series of culverts before draining into the lake's south edge. Public golf courses, a stone house begun in 1748, a family burial ground, a parade ground, a stadium and named trails share the ground with 301 bird species recorded since 1875 and mammals including white-tailed deer, raccoons, Eastern coyotes and wild turkeys. The Van Cortlandt family sold the property to the City of New York in 1888. NYC Parks owns it and manages it with assistance from the Van Cortlandt Park Alliance.

sections.heading: What's in the park
sections.body:
The Van Cortlandt House stands in the southwestern corner of the park, near the Riverdale neighborhood: a 2½-story Georgian building with a rubblestone facade, L-shaped, with wings extending along the south and east sides. It is the oldest known surviving house in the Bronx. Keystones above its windows are carved as grotesque masks, several fireplaces are set with Dutch tiles, and a U-shaped stairway in the front hall carries turned balusters. It has been open to the public as a museum since May 28, 1897, and is operated by the National Society of Colonial Dames in the State of New York.

The Van Cortlandt Golf Course and the Mosholu Golf Course sit inside the park, both run by NYC Parks. The Van Cortlandt Golf Course opened on July 6, 1895 as a nine-hole course, expanded to eighteen holes in 1899, and its clubhouse dates to 1902; it is the oldest public golf course in the United States and is frequently called Vanny or Vannie. The park's own article credits Tom Bendelow, nicknamed the "Johnny Appleseed of Golf", with expanding it to 18 holes, and records a renovation in 2016. The clubhouse locker room was a filming location for the 1987 film Wall Street. Mosholu Golf Course was built in 1914, originally designed as an eighteen-hole course and now nine due to road construction; its driving range and putting green also function as a water treatment plant, and it is adjacent to the Woodlawn station on the IRT Jerome Avenue Line. Beneath that driving range, 160 feet underground, is the Croton Water Filtration Plant, which measures 830 by 550 feet — larger than Yankee Stadium — and processes up to 320 million gallons a day.

The Putnam Trail is 1.5 miles and rated easy, following the former New York and Putnam Railroad railbed and connecting to the South County Trailway; it was reconstructed in 2019 and 2020. The Old Croton Aqueduct Trail runs 1.1 miles and is rated easy to moderate; the Old Croton Trail enters New York City on the eastern side of Van Cortlandt Park. The John Kieran Nature Trail, 1.25 miles and rated easy, opened in 1987 and passes 13 stone pillars tested for the facade of Grand Central Terminal. The John Muir Trail, 1.5 miles and rated moderate, was established in 1997 and is the park's only east–west trail, connecting the three northern forested areas. The Cass Gallagher Nature Trail, 1.4 miles and rated moderate to difficult, is the hardest trail in the park: a loop through the rocky forests of the park's northwestern portion, given its current name in 1984 and repeatedly crossing a 3-mile cross-country trail.

Vault Hill, the Van Cortlandt family burial ground, was created in 1749 and holds the remains of Frederick Van Cortlandt. The Parade Ground began as grain fields and was converted into a sprawling lawn, used by the National Guard for brigade practice and later for recreational facilities and concerts; it was restored with construction-mitigation funds from the Croton Water Filtration Plant project, which also paid for the Sachkerah Woods Playground at the park's southeast corner. Van Cortlandt Stadium was added in 1939 on the site of a former swamp, and a pool followed in 1970. In the northeast of the park is Indian Field, where the Stockbridge Militia was attacked in August 1778.

sections.heading: The Van Cortlandts, the Revolution and the city park
sections.body:
Jacobus Van Cortlandt purchased the land from John Barrett around 1691. In 1699 he dammed Tibbetts Brook to power a sawmill and gristmill, creating the mill pond that became Van Cortlandt Lake. Frederick Van Cortlandt began developing the Van Cortlandt House on the property in 1748. He died before the house was finished; his will, signed on October 2, 1749, indicated that the house was almost complete, and he bequeathed the estate to his son Jacobus (James) Van Cortlandt. A family burial ground was created in 1749, later to be known as Vault Hill, and Frederick was buried there.

The property was used during the American Revolution between 1776 and 1783, by both Patriot and British forces. The house served as Washington's headquarters after his troops were defeated in the 1776 Battle of Long Island; the British general William Howe made it his headquarters on November 13, 1776; Washington stayed there again before the Battle of White Plains and returned in 1781 and 1783. In 1781 he came back to strategize with Rochambeau while their troops waited on what is now the Parade Ground and Vault Hill. Augustus Van Cortlandt hid city records under Vault Hill to protect them during the war, turning them over to the new American government afterward.

In August 1778, at Indian Field in the northeast of the park, approximately one mile north of Kingsbridge, the Stockbridge Militia was attacked in a cavalry charge by the Queen's Rangers, a Loyalist unit commanded by Lieutenant Colonel John Graves Simcoe. The militia was a Native American unit of Mohican, Wappinger, Munsee, Tunxis, Shawnee and Housatonic people serving the Continental Army under Jehoiaikim Mtohksin and Abraham Nimham. By most accounts roughly 40 Stockbridge Militia were killed, while the Queen's Rangers suffered 1 cavalryman killed and 3 wounded. Survivors were discharged by Washington's order in September 1778 and paid $1,000.

The family sold the property to the City of New York in 1888 and it was converted to public parkland; the golf course followed on July 6, 1895. Between the 1930s and 1955 Robert Moses directed construction of the Henry Hudson and Mosholu Parkways, fragmenting the park into six pieces. The 1975 New York City fiscal crisis caused much of the park to fall into disrepair. A "Van Cortlandt Park Master Plan 2034" was published in 2014.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Woodlawn, at Bainbridge Avenue and Jerome Avenue in Norwood, outside Woodlawn Cemetery, is the northern terminus of the IRT Jerome Avenue Line and is served by the 4 at all times. It opened on April 15, 1918, built by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company as part of the Dual Contracts, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places following 2005 renovations for its ornamental concrete design. It is not ADA-accessible, and the MTA announced in July 2025 that it would install elevators there. Its connecting buses are the Bx16, Bx34, BxM4 and Bee-Line Routes 4, 20 and 21.

Van Cortlandt Park–242nd Street, at West 242nd Street and Broadway on the border of Fieldston and Kingsbridge, is the northern terminal of its line and is served exclusively by the 1; the next stop to the south is 238th Street. It opened on August 1, 1908 as part of the Contract 1 system, designed by Heins & LaFarge in Victorian Gothic style, and is the only elevated terminal station left in that style from Contract 1. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on March 30, 2005, reference #05000226. It is not ADA-accessible; an elevator contract was awarded in December 2023, with construction anticipated to complete in 2026. Its connecting buses are the Bx9, BxM3 and Bee-Line Routes 1, 2 and 3.

Bus routes serving the park are the Bx9, Bx10, Bx16 and Bx34; the BxM3 and BxM4 express routes; and Bee-Line Routes 1, 2, 3, 4, 20 and 21.

The New York and Putnam Railroad's main line once ran through the park. Its main-line passenger service ended on May 29, 1958, and the corridor is now the Putnam Trail; the skeletal remains of Van Cortlandt station and a milepost marker, Milepost 6, are still in the park.

faq.question: How do I get to Van Cortlandt Park?
faq.answer: Woodlawn, at Bainbridge Avenue and Jerome Avenue in Norwood, outside Woodlawn Cemetery, is the northern terminus of the IRT Jerome Avenue Line and is served by the 4 at all times; its connecting buses are the Bx16, Bx34, BxM4 and Bee-Line Routes 4, 20 and 21. Van Cortlandt Park–242nd Street, at West 242nd Street and Broadway, is the northern terminal of its line and is served exclusively by the 1; its connecting buses are the Bx9, BxM3 and Bee-Line Routes 1, 2 and 3. Bus routes serving the park are the Bx9, Bx10, Bx16 and Bx34, the BxM3 and BxM4 express routes, and Bee-Line Routes 1, 2, 3, 4, 20 and 21. Neither subway station is ADA-accessible.

faq.question: How big is Van Cortlandt Park?
faq.answer: 1,146 acres (464 ha), which makes it the third-largest park in New York City, behind the Staten Island Greenbelt at 1,778 acres and Pelham Bay Park at 2,772 acres. Between the 1930s and 1955 Robert Moses directed construction of the Henry Hudson and Mosholu Parkways, which fragmented the park into six pieces.

faq.question: What is the Van Cortlandt House Museum?
faq.answer: A 2½-story Georgian house with a rubblestone facade in the park's southwestern corner, the oldest known surviving house in the Bronx. Frederick Van Cortlandt began developing it in 1748 and died before it was finished; his will, signed on October 2, 1749, indicated the house was almost complete, and his son Jacobus (James) inherited it. It was Washington's headquarters after the 1776 Battle of Long Island and General Howe's from November 13, 1776. New York City acquired it in 1888, it served as police and military barracks, and it opened as a museum on May 28, 1897. Its exterior was designated a New York City Landmark on March 15, 1966 and its interior on July 22, 1975.

The John Muir Trail, 1.5 miles and rated moderate, is the park's only east–west trail. The Cass Gallagher Nature Trail, 1.4 miles and rated moderate to difficult, is the hardest trail in the park.

faq.question: What happened at Indian Field?
faq.answer: In August 1778 the Stockbridge Militia — a Native American unit of Mohican, Wappinger, Munsee, Tunxis, Shawnee and Housatonic people serving the Continental Army under Jehoiaikim Mtohksin and Abraham Nimham — was attacked at Indian Field, in the northeast of what is now Van Cortlandt Park, by the Queen's Rangers under Lieutenant Colonel John Graves Simcoe, in a cavalry charge. By most accounts roughly 40 Stockbridge Militia were killed; the Queen's Rangers suffered 1 cavalryman killed and 3 wounded. Survivors were discharged by Washington's order in September 1778 and paid $1,000.

photos.title: The Parade Ground, Van Cortlandt Park
photos.description: A wide, flat expanse of sun-bleached grass under a clear blue sky, photographed from the shade of a tree with a concrete path along the bottom edge. Soccer goals, a chain-link backstop, a mound of bare earth and small groups of players in coloured kit line the far side of the field, with a long wooded ridge rising behind them.
photos.author: Dmadeo

places.name: Van Cortlandt House Museum
places.summary: A 2½-story Georgian house with a rubblestone facade in the southwestern corner of Van Cortlandt Park, near the Riverdale neighborhood, L-shaped with wings extending along the south and east sides. It is the oldest known surviving house in the Bronx. Keystones above the windows are carved as grotesque masks, several fireplaces are set with Dutch tiles, and a U-shaped stairway in the front hall carries turned balusters.
places.history:
Frederick Van Cortlandt began developing the house on the property in 1748. He died before it was finished; his will, signed on October 2, 1749, indicated that the house was almost complete, and he bequeathed the estate to his son Jacobus (James) Van Cortlandt.

The house was used by both Patriot and British forces during the Revolution. It served as Washington's headquarters after his troops were defeated in the 1776 Battle of Long Island; the British general William Howe made it his headquarters on November 13, 1776; Washington stayed there again before the Battle of White Plains and returned in 1781 and 1783. In 1781 he came back to strategize with Rochambeau while their troops waited on what is now the Parade Ground and Vault Hill.

New York City acquired the house in 1888 and it served as police and military barracks before opening to the public as a museum on May 28, 1897, under the Society of Colonial Dames of the State of New York — the same body, under its later name, that operates it now: as of 2023 the National Society of Colonial Dames in the State of New York.

Its exterior was designated a New York City Landmark on March 15, 1966 and its interior on July 22, 1975. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 24, 1967 and designated a National Historic Landmark on December 24, 1976.

photos.title: Van Cortlandt House Museum
photos.description: The front of the Van Cortlandt House on a clear day: a rubblestone facade laid up with brick surrounds, white-framed sash windows on two floors, three dormers in the slate-grey roof, and a small columned porch reached by a flight of steps.
photos.author: Dmadeo

places.name: Vault Hill
places.summary: The Van Cortlandt family burial ground inside Van Cortlandt Park, created in 1749 and holding the remains of Frederick Van Cortlandt.
places.history: Augustus Van Cortlandt hid city records under Vault Hill to protect them during the Revolutionary War, turning them over to the new American government after the war. In 1781 Washington's and Rochambeau's troops waited on what is now the Parade Ground and Vault Hill while the generals strategized inside the Van Cortlandt House. The hill's headstones and crypts were vandalized in the 1960s, noted by a New York Times reader as early as 1962.

places.name: Van Cortlandt Golf Course
places.summary: A public golf course inside Van Cortlandt Park, operated by the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation and frequently called Vanny or Vannie. It is the oldest public golf course in the United States.
places.history: It opened on July 6, 1895 as a nine-hole course and was expanded to eighteen holes in 1899; the clubhouse dates to 1902. The park's own article credits Tom Bendelow, nicknamed the "Johnny Appleseed of Golf", with expanding it to 18 holes, and records a renovation in 2016. The clubhouse locker room was a filming location for the 1987 film Wall Street.

photos.title: Van Cortlandt Golf Course clubhouse sign
photos.description: A painted board mounted on the stuccoed clubhouse wall above a white-framed doorway, lettered "Van Cortlandt Golf Course / America's Oldest Public Golf Course" with "Established 1895" beneath and a circular leaf emblem beside it.
photos.author: Shannon McGee

places.name: Mosholu Golf Course
places.summary: A public golf course at Van Cortlandt Park, built in 1914. It was originally designed as an eighteen-hole course and is now nine due to road construction. Its driving range and putting green also function as a water treatment plant, and it is adjacent to the Woodlawn station on the IRT Jerome Avenue Line, served by the 4.
places.history: It is also called the Mosholu Links. The Croton Water Filtration Plant was built 160 feet underground beneath its driving range.

places.name: Van Cortlandt Lake
places.summary: The largest freshwater lake in the Bronx: 18 acres, 4 to 8 feet deep, inside Van Cortlandt Park. Largemouth bass, carp, perch and catfish have been recorded in it. It is fed by Tibbetts Brook, a stream originating in Yonkers which runs through a series of culverts before draining into the south edge of the lake.
places.history: Jacobus Van Cortlandt dammed Tibbetts Brook in 1699 to power a sawmill and gristmill, creating the lake as a mill pond. It faced severe pollution between the 1960s and the 1980s, and restoration began in 1978.

photos.title: Van Cortlandt Lake
photos.description: Van Cortlandt Lake under an overcast sky in early spring, photographed from a rocky bank with bare branches leaning over the water. Leafless woods line the far shore, with a paved path and parked cars visible along the right-hand bank.
photos.author: Mbochart

places.name: Putnam Trail
places.summary: A 1.5-mile trail through Van Cortlandt Park, rated easy, following the former New York and Putnam Railroad railbed and connecting to the South County Trailway. It was reconstructed in 2019 and 2020.
places.history: The New York and Putnam Railroad's main line ran along this corridor, and its main-line passenger service ended on May 29, 1958. The skeletal remains of Van Cortlandt station and a milepost marker, Milepost 6, are still in the park. The former right-of-way north of the old station was converted into the Putnam Greenway, South County Trailway, North County Trailway and Putnam County Trailway.

places.name: Old Croton Aqueduct Trail
places.summary: A 1.1-mile trail through Van Cortlandt Park along the route of the Old Croton Aqueduct, rated easy to moderate. The Old Croton Trail enters New York City on the eastern side of Van Cortlandt Park.
places.history: The aqueduct was built between 1837 and 1842; water began flowing on June 22, 1842 and it opened to the public on October 14, 1842. The original system's service ended in 1955, and portions reopened in 1987. The New Croton Aqueduct opened in 1890. The Old Croton Aqueduct was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 2, 1974 and designated a National Historic Landmark on April 27, 1992, a designation extended to cover the aqueduct's route in the Bronx.

places.name: John Kieran Nature Trail
places.summary: A 1.25-mile nature trail in Van Cortlandt Park, rated easy, which opened in 1987. It passes 13 stone pillars tested for the facade of Grand Central Terminal.

places.name: John Muir Trail
places.summary: A 1.5-mile trail in Van Cortlandt Park, rated moderate, established in 1997. It is the park's only east–west trail, connecting the three northern forested areas.

places.name: Cass Gallagher Nature Trail
places.summary: A 1.4-mile loop through the rocky forests of Van Cortlandt Park's northwestern portion, rated moderate to difficult and the hardest trail in the park. It repeatedly crosses a 3-mile cross-country trail.
places.history: It was given its current name in 1984, and was historically a self-guided interpretive nature trail.

places.name: Parade Ground
places.summary: A sprawling lawn in Van Cortlandt Park, originally grain fields. The National Guard used it for brigade practice, and it has hosted recreational facilities and concerts.
places.history: In 1781 Washington's and Rochambeau's troops waited on what is now the Parade Ground and Vault Hill while the generals strategized inside the Van Cortlandt House. The lawn was restored using construction-mitigation funds from the Croton Water Filtration Plant project.

places.name: Croton Water Filtration Plant
places.summary: A filtration plant built 160 feet underground beneath the Mosholu Golf Course driving range in Van Cortlandt Park. It measures 830 by 550 feet — larger than Yankee Stadium — processes up to 320 million gallons per day, is designed to remove 99.9% of Giardia cysts, Cryptosporidium and viruses, and supplies roughly 10% of New York City's water.
places.history: Construction ran from 2007 to 2015 and the plant was activated in May 2015. It was projected at $800 million and its final cost reached $3.2 billion, due to delays and community opposition; a contemporary headline ran "Plan to Put Filtration Plant Under Park Angers the Bronx". Mitigation funds from the project restored the park's Parade Ground and built the Sachkerah Woods Playground.

places.name: Indian Field
places.summary: The site in the northeast of Van Cortlandt Park, approximately one mile north of Kingsbridge, where the Stockbridge Militia was attacked in August 1778.
places.history: The Stockbridge Militia was a Native American unit of Mohican, Wappinger, Munsee, Tunxis, Shawnee and Housatonic people serving the Continental Army under Jehoiaikim Mtohksin and Abraham Nimham. It was attacked in a cavalry charge by the Queen's Rangers, a Loyalist unit commanded by Lieutenant Colonel John Graves Simcoe. By most accounts roughly 40 Stockbridge Militia were killed, while the Queen's Rangers suffered 1 cavalryman killed and 3 wounded. Survivors were discharged by Washington's order in September 1778 and paid $1,000.

places.name: Sachkerah Woods Playground
places.summary: A playground at Van Cortlandt Park's southeast corner, built as a construction-mitigation project of the Croton Water Filtration Plant.

places.name: Van Cortlandt Stadium
places.summary: A stadium in Van Cortlandt Park, added in 1939 on the site of a former swamp. A pool followed in 1970.
